opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, it's great to be here.

That paper is one I'm still quite proud of, mainly because of the timing. When we started around 2017, deep reinforcement learning was producing striking results, but almost all of them were in simulation: animated characters, MuJoCo humanoids, and so on. Most roboticists, including many of my colleagues, were skeptical that any of it would transfer to a physical robot. The common view was that the "reality gap" was too big. Simulators were too idealized, and policies would exploit physics artifacts that didn't exist in the real world.

What we tried to show with the Minitaur, the small quadruped we were using, was that the gap could be closed systematically rather than by luck. We did a few fairly simple things. We built a much more accurate actuator model by identifying the motor dynamics. We modeled latency, which turned out to matter a great deal and which people often overlooked. And we used dynamics randomization, varying mass, friction, motor strength, and so on during training, so the policy became robust instead of overfitting to one simulator. With those pieces, policies trained entirely in PyBullet could trot and gallop on the real robot without any fine-tuning on hardware.

As for impact, I'd be careful not to overclaim. We were one of several groups working on this at the same time, and the ideas weren't entirely new; domain randomization was also being explored by OpenAI and others. I think our contribution was to give an early, concrete demonstration on a legged robot, which is a hard, contact-rich, unstable system, that sim-to-real with learned controllers was practical. That helped shift the field's attitude from "learning on legged robots is a toy" to "this could be the main way we build locomotion controllers."

Looking at where things are now, it's very satisfying. Most of the impressive quadruped and humanoid locomotion you see today, from ETH Zurich's ANYmal work, from Berkeley, from many companies, follows essentially the same recipe: massive simulation, randomization, careful modeling of the hardware, then zero-shot transfer. The tools have become much better, with GPU-parallel simulators like Isaac Gym letting you train in minutes what took us days. But the basic philosophy, that simulation is the data engine for robot learning, is something I think that paper helped establish.

It also shaped my own thinking. It convinced me that the bottleneck in robotics is largely data, and that simulation is one of the most scalable ways to get it. Much of my later work follows from that.

r001.rationale: The response says the paper helped shift the field’s attitude, but does not describe reinforcement learning as robotics’ first paradigm shift in roughly a decade.

r002.rationale: It says current quadruped and humanoid locomotion work follows the paper’s recipe of simulation, hardware modeling, randomization, and zero-shot transfer, and describes the learned controllers as reinforcement-learning policies.

r003.rationale: It calls the work an early concrete demonstration of sim-to-real learned control on a legged robot, but does not say the paper pioneered combining reinforcement learning and Sim2Real for quadrupeds; it also notes several groups were working on it at the same time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That paper has a special place for me, because it was really where my work on legged robots at Google began, and it also, I think, marked a turning point for how the field approached locomotion.

To put it in context: before that, most quadruped locomotion was built on carefully engineered controllers, model-based methods, lots of hand tuning. Reinforcement learning in simulation looked promising, but almost everyone ran into the same wall, which is that policies trained in simulation would fall apart the moment you put them on a real robot. The dynamics never matched, the motors behaved differently, the contacts were off, latency wasn't modeled. People called it the "reality gap," and for a while it felt like a fundamental barrier rather than an engineering problem.

What we tried to show in that paper was that the gap could actually be closed in a systematic way. We did a few things together: we built a much more accurate actuator model, because the motors turned out to be one of the biggest sources of mismatch; we measured and modeled latency carefully; and we added randomization and perturbations during training so the policy learned to be robust rather than overfit to one idealized simulator. Then we trained gaits like trotting and galloping entirely in simulation and deployed them on the Minitaur robot with no additional training in the real world. Seeing the robot actually run with a policy that had never touched reality before was a genuinely exciting moment for the team.

In terms of impact, I'd point to a few things. First, it gave the community confidence that sim-to-real transfer for legged locomotion was feasible, and I think it encouraged a lot of groups to take that path seriously. The approach of accurate system identification plus domain randomization became something of a standard recipe, and you see versions of it in a lot of the work that followed, including later results on much more capable robots like ANYmal and the Unitree platforms doing very dynamic, robust behaviors. Second, it helped shift the mindset from "the simulator is a toy" to "the simulator is a training ground," which really changed how people allocate their effort. Now a great deal of robotics research is about building better simulators and better transfer methods rather than hand-designing controllers.

That said, I want to be honest about its limits. The paper was a proof of concept. The behaviors were relatively simple, the robot was a fairly small platform, and we didn't address perception or complex terrain. Many of the truly impressive advances came from others building on and going well beyond what we did. So I'd say its contribution was less about solving the problem and more about opening a door and demonstrating a methodology that turned out to be scalable.

Personally, it also shaped everything I did afterward. It led directly to work on learning locomotion in the real world, on learning from animal motion data, and more recently on using large models for robot control. So in that sense, its biggest impact on me was that it set the direction for the next several years of my research.

r001.rationale: The response calls the paper a turning point for locomotion, but does not describe reinforcement learning as robotics’ first paradigm shift in roughly a decade.

r002.rationale: It says the paper encouraged groups to pursue sim-to-real transfer and mentions later dynamic behaviors, but does not attribute the widespread emergence of agile robot capabilities to adopting reinforcement learning and Sim2Real.

r003.rationale: The response describes training quadruped gaits in simulation and deploying them on a real robot, but does not clearly say the paper pioneered combining reinforcement learning and Sim2Real for quadrupeds.

astra-6.text:
I think its main impact was helping show that a locomotion policy learned in simulation could transfer to a real quadruped and produce agile behavior. That made simulation more compelling as a practical tool for developing robot controllers.

The challenge is that a policy can work beautifully in simulation and still fail on hardware. So the important question is how to train something that remains effective when the real robot behaves differently from the simulator.

I would put the paper’s contribution in that broader context. It was one step toward making learning-based locomotion practical, and toward a workflow where we can do much of the learning in simulation and then bring those capabilities to a physical robot.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as an early step toward making reinforcement learning useful on real robots. The central idea was to learn agile locomotion in simulation and then transfer that policy to a physical quadruped. That matters because simulation lets you explore and learn without putting all of that burden on the hardware.

I wouldn’t attribute the field’s progress to one paper, but I think it helped build confidence in that approach. It also highlighted that learning a policy is only part of the problem—you have to address the gap between simulation and the real world. For me, that was an important direction for robotics: using simulation as a practical tool for developing behaviors that work outside it.

r001.rationale: The response calls the paper an early step toward useful reinforcement learning on real robots, but does not describe it as robotics’ first paradigm shift in roughly a decade.

r002.rationale: It discusses agile locomotion and simulation-to-real transfer, but does not attribute the widespread emergence of agile robot capabilities to adopting reinforcement learning and Sim2Real.

r003.rationale: It describes learning locomotion in simulation and transferring the policy to a quadruped, but does not say the paper pioneered combining reinforcement learning and Sim2Real for quadrupeds.
